title: Why Can't You Ever Reach a Rainbow? #rainbow #physics
description:
A rainbow isn't a thing in the sky: it's an angle. Light leaving raindrops bunches up about 42° from the path the sunlight came in on, so you only see colour from drops about 42° from the shadow of your head. Move, and a different set of drops lights up.

Full episode: Why is a rainbow always at the same angle? https://youtu.be/CywvAndxdSk

Sources
- HyperPhysics (Georgia State University), Rainbow
- Cowley, Atmospheric Optics, Rainbows
- Nussenzveig (1977), The theory of the rainbow, Scientific American 236(4)
- Minnaert, Light and Colour in the Outdoors, Springer

Have you ever seen a double rainbow? Tell me in the comments.

Script, voice and animation are AI-produced (Claude; Kokoro voice). Every number is checked against the sources above.

subtitles: Why can't you ever reach a rainbow?
Walk toward one, and it backs away.
Step sideways, and it follows you.
That's because a rainbow isn't a thing in the sky.
Some sunlight enters a raindrop, bends, bounces off the back, and comes out again.
It comes back out bunched up about 42° from the path the sunlight came in on.
Each colour bends a little differently, so red and violet come out at slightly different angles.
So the rainbow is made by drops about 42° from the shadow of your head, as seen from your eye.
Take a step, and a different set of drops lights up.
You can't reach it, because it's always 42° away.
